JATAYU, who was fast asleep, awoke on hearing these words 
and beheld Ravana and the daughter of Videha. 
Thereupon, the King of Birds, with his sharp beak resembling 
the peak of a mountain, perching on the tree, spoke softly to 
Ravana, saying :-
" 0 Dashagriva, I am conversant with the Puranas, firm in 
my vows, and follow the path of dharma. 
0 Brother, it does 
not become thee to commit this infamy in my presence ! My 
name is Jatayu, the King of the Vultures ; she whom thou dost 
seek to bear away is the beautiful Sita, the faithful and illustrious 
conson of the ProteCtor of the Worlds, that Lord of Men, 
Rama, the son of Dasaratha, who is equal to Varuna and 
Mahendra and ever engaged in the welfare of all beings. 
"How can a king, fixed in his duty, look upon another's 
wife ? 0 Thou of mighty prowess, it is for thee particularly 
to defend the consons of kings, therefore control thy base 
inclination to insult the wife of another. A noble person will 
ever eschew that which may bring reproach on him, and 
protects another's wife as if she were his own. 
" 0 Delight of Poulastya, whether it concerns that which is 
expedient or agreeable, in the absence of the authority of the 
scriptures, men of honour follow the example of a king in 
matters of duty. A king represents duty, a king represents 
desire and is the supreme ueasucy of his subjects ; he is the 
root of good and evil. 
" 0 King of the Titans, thou art wicked and fickle by nature; 
how hast thou obtained a kingdom, like unto a sinner winning 
the celestial abode ? It is haed for an unruly and passionate 
man to change his nature ; noble counsels are not long remem-
bered by perverse persons. Since the mighty and virtuous 
Rama has never done a wrong in thy kingdnm or capital, 
why dost thou seek to provoke him ? Is Rama of irreproach-

" 0 Ravana, tbou an unwittingly carrying a highly venomous

" 0 Ravana, I am sixty tbousand years old and have ruled 
over tbe domain of mine ancestors witb justice. I am exceed-
ingly aged, tbou an youthful and furnished witb a bow, annour 
and arrows, mounted on a car, yet tbou shalt not escape 
without injury, if thou seekest to bear Vaidehi away. Thou 
shalt no more be able to cony her away by force in my presence,

" If tbou an not afraid, 0 Ravana, tben halt an instant and 
fight ! Tbou shalt fall on the eanh as Khara before tbee I 
Ramo, clad in robes of bark, who more than once vanquished 
the Daityas and Danavas in tbe field, would soon have slain 
tbee in combat. As for me, what can I do ? The two princes 
are far away and undoubtedly tbou an fleeing in all haste in 
fear of tbem, Tbou Wretch! Yet while I still live, tbou shalt 
not bear away tbe lovely Sita, the beloved consort of Ramo, 
whose eyes resemble tbe petals of tbe lotus. Even at the

Ramo, as if to King Dasaratba himself. 
Stay ! Stay I 0

brief.summary_1line: The aged vulture king Jatayu confronts Ravana, condemns the abduction of Sita, and challenges him to battle to defend Rama’s wife.

image_candidates.scene_text: The aged vulture king Jatayu perches on a tree, wings spread and beak raised, confronting Ravana in his chariot as Sita looks on in distress.
Jatayu, towering with ragged wings and fierce eyes, challenges the armored Ravana carrying Sita in a golden chariot in the forest sky.
The ancient bird king stands defiantly before Ravana’s chariot, declaring his challenge while the forest winds whip around Sita’s flowing garments.

deep.rich_summary: As Ravana abducts Sita and carries her away, the aged vulture-king Jatayu awakens and confronts the demon king. Perched above them, Jatayu rebukes Ravana with a long moral warning, invoking dharma and the duties of kings. He reminds Ravana that Sita is the faithful wife of Rama, a righteous ruler whose wrath will be terrible. Jatayu denounces Ravana’s act as shameful, predicting that abducting Sita is like carrying a deadly serpent or wearing the noose of death. Though extremely old, he declares he will fight to protect her out of loyalty to Rama and King Dasaratha. The scene marks the first heroic resistance to the abduction, highlighting dharma, courage, and the coming clash between Ravana and Rama.

highlight_spans.why: Jatayu awakens and recognizes Ravana with Sita, establishing the divine witness who will challenge the abduction.
Jatayu proclaims Sita as Rama’s faithful consort and invokes Rama’s divine stature, framing the moral gravity of Ravana’s crime.
The vivid metaphor comparing Ravana’s act to carrying a venomous serpent or wearing the noose of death foreshadows his destruction.
The aged Jatayu declares he will risk his life to defend Sita for Rama’s sake, turning the confrontation into a moment of sacrificial heroism.
Jatayu openly challenges Ravana to stop and fight, transforming moral protest into the beginning of a mythic battle.

top_scenes.scene_text: The colossal vulture-king Jatayu perched on a towering tree spreads his wings and confronts Ravana’s chariot as the demon carries the struggling Sita through the forest sky.
Jatayu, ancient yet fierce, points his sharp mountain-like beak toward Ravana while delivering a thunderous warning as Sita watches with desperate hope.
Ravana’s ornate flying chariot races through the air with Sita in captivity while the giant bird Jatayu launches from a treetop to block its path.
